overview: This file concerns F. W. Lee’s attempt to recover value from eleven 1931 bonds of the Taiwan Electric Company, which were underwritten by J. P. Morgan & Company and guaranteed by the Japanese Government. Senator Millard E. Tydings forwarded Lee’s inquiry to Secretary of State Dean Acheson, mistakenly reporting that the company’s property was in U.S. federal possession. The Department of State replied that the company operated in Taiwan, then administered by the Chinese Government, and that Congress had not yet determined whether such Japanese-guaranteed securities could be satisfied from vested Japanese assets in the United States. It directed Lee toward the Foreign Bondholders Protective Council while explaining the Department’s general policy that foreign securities were private investments whose owners primarily bore their associated risks.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Tydings concerning F. W. Lee’s Taiwan Electric Company bonds
subfiles.from: Ernest A. Gross, Assistant Secretary of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Millard E. Tydings, United States Senate
subfiles.about: The Department explains the uncertain legal and diplomatic status of F. W. Lee’s Japanese-guaranteed Taiwan Electric Company bonds and recommends that he work through the Foreign Bondholders Protective Council.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that Lee’s eleven bonds formed part of a July 1, 1931 issue underwritten by J. P. Morgan & Company and guaranteed by the Japanese Government. Whether such securities could be paid from vested Japanese assets remained for Congress to determine following recommendations from the War Claims Commission, apart from the limited provisions of Public Law No. 671. The company’s property was in Taiwan under Chinese administration rather than in U.S. possession, and the Department was seeking information from the American Consulate General at Taipei. The letter directs Lee to the Foreign Bondholders Protective Council and emphasizes that foreign securities are fundamentally private investments, although the government may provide appropriate assistance.

subfiles.title: Senator Tydings’s inquiry to Secretary Acheson about F. W. Lee’s bond claim
subfiles.from: Millard E. Tydings, chairman, Senate Committee on Armed Services
subfiles.about: Senator Tydings asks the State Department for information about a constituent’s claim involving eleven Taiwan Electric Company bonds.
subfiles.summary: Tydings reports that F. W. Lee said he had filed a claim in 1945 or 1946 for eleven Taiwan Electric Company bonds purchased in New York around 1935. Lee stated that payments continued until December 1942 and believed that the company remained active and its property was in federal possession. Tydings asks Acheson for information that he can transmit to Lee.

interest: The file offers a compact case study of how prewar Japanese-guaranteed debt became entangled with postwar claims policy, vested enemy assets, and Taiwan’s transfer to Chinese administration. It is particularly useful for showing how the State Department distinguished assets located in Taiwan from Japanese property held in the United States and how it treated foreign securities as private risks while still assisting bondholders through a quasi-public protective council. The paired letters also reveal the role of congressional constituent service—and the misunderstandings it could transmit—in shaping official explanations of unsettled international financial claims.
